# Viewing Thurston geometries from inside

An in-space view follows light rays from an observer inside a geometry.
The ray-marching backend supports the eight homogeneous
three-dimensional geometries studied by Thurston. This article renders
an intrinsic scene in each space, following the construction of Coulon,
Matsumoto, Segerman and Trettel
[2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15801). Installation is covered in
[Get started](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/ggplot3d.md).
[Plotting curved spaces and
spacetime](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/curved-spaces.md)
introduces the exterior coordinate views.

``` r

library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
```

## Positioning objects from the observer

A geodesic is the path followed by a freely travelling ray in a
geometry. Place three balls by travelling along three initial directions
from the origin. Their centres are at intrinsic distances of 1.5, 1.9
and 2.2 units, and their radii are 0.22, 0.28 and 0.28. The same
directions, distances and radii are used in each scene, so changes in
appearance come from the geometry.

``` r

directions <- rbind(c(-0.4, -0.15, 1), c(0.3, 0.2, 1), c(0.1, -0.25, 1))
distances <- c(1.5, 1.9, 2.2)
radii <- c(0.22, 0.28, 0.28)
colours <- c("#2E6F9E", "#9E5E0F", "#3F7A3D")
inside <- function(geometry) {
  balls <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
    centre <- geodesic_3d(geometry, direction = directions[i, ],
      distance = distances[i])$position
    annotation_thurston_3d(centre = as.numeric(centre), radius = radii[i],
      fill = colours[i])
  })
  ggplot() + balls + theme_void() +
    coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", geometry = geometry,
      dpi = 52, antialias = 1, max_distance = 3.5, max_steps = 256))
}
```

The initial observer is the origin and the view points along its
positive third frame direction. Intrinsic primitives use their
geometry’s chart coordinates. Ordinary point, path and mesh layers are
rejected by this backend; use balls, cylinders, half-spaces or
chart-defined traced SDFs.

## Euclidean space

Euclidean space has the familiar flat metric. Rays are straight and the
angular size of a small ball decreases with its distance. The three
balls provide a reference for the curved spaces below.

``` r

inside("e3")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Spherical space

Spherical three-space has positive curvature. Neighbouring rays can
reconverge, and geodesics return after a full circuit. Its stereographic
chart represents the space in three coordinates; the renderer follows
the intrinsic rays across the chart’s pole. The more distant balls
occupy larger angular regions in this scene.

``` r

inside("s3")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Hyperbolic space

Hyperbolic three-space has negative curvature. Neighbouring rays
diverge, which makes distant balls occupy smaller angles. Coordinates
use the open Poincare ball: every centre and observer must have
Euclidean norm below one. The geodesic positioning above supplies valid
chart coordinates.

``` r

inside("h3")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Spherical plane times a line

The product of a sphere and a Euclidean line curves the first two
directions and leaves the third direction flat. Rays can reconverge in
the spherical factor while separating along the line. This directional
dependence changes the apparent outlines of balls viewed obliquely to
the line.

``` r

inside("s2xe")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Hyperbolic plane times a line

The product of a hyperbolic plane and a Euclidean line expands ray
separations in its curved factor. Its line direction remains flat. The
first two chart coordinates lie in the open Poincare disk, and the third
records distance along the line.

``` r

inside("h2xe")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Nil

Nil couples horizontal movement to the vertical coordinate. A horizontal
loop can produce vertical displacement, and geodesics with a vertical
component curve in the horizontal directions. The chart uses ordinary
three-component coordinates with this coupled distance rule. Intrinsic
balls can have asymmetric apparent outlines away from the viewing axis.

``` r

inside("nil")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Sol

Sol stretches one horizontal direction and contracts the other as height
changes. Rotating a viewing direction therefore changes how rays
separate and how a surface appears. The ball primitive here uses the
approximate level set described in section 11.5 of Coulon and
colleagues, with horizontal weights that vary exponentially with height.
These shapes illustrate that approximation; their level-set definition
is approximate.

``` r

inside("sol")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The universal cover of SL(2, R)

This geometry combines a hyperbolic base with an unwrapped fibre
direction. The fibre records a continuously accumulated rotation;
travelling around the base changes that rotation. The chart uses two
hyperboloid coordinates and the unwrapped fibre coordinate. The
renderer’s geodesics and distance calculation account for the coupling.

``` r

inside("sl2r")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Moving and turning the observer

Set the observer location and orientation on
[`backend_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/backend_3d.md).
The columns of `facing` are the right, up and forward unit tangent
vectors in the observer’s orthonormal frame. The example below moves
sideways in Nil and turns by five degrees. The backend’s field of view
controls the full-panel perspective image; the exterior camera’s azimuth
and elevation do not set this view.

``` r

angle <- 5 * pi / 180
facing <- matrix(c(cos(angle), 0, -sin(angle), 0, 1, 0,
  sin(angle), 0, cos(angle)), 3, 3)
inside("nil") + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", geometry = "nil",
  observer = c(0.05, 0, 0), facing = facing, fov = 90,
  dpi = 52, antialias = 1, max_distance = 3.5, max_steps = 256))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The light is located at the observer. Its diffuse intensity depends on
the area density of geodesic spheres along the viewing ray. Use the
ambient and diffuse strengths of
[`light_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/light_3d.md)
to adjust illumination. The maximum ray length and step count bound the
rendering work; small distant objects may need a longer range or more
steps.

## Following a ray numerically

The same geodesic kernel is available for numerical inspection. Its
result contains positions, orthonormal-frame velocities, coordinate
velocities, parallel-transport matrices and area densities. For a
Euclidean ray the area density grows as squared distance; the following
output compares it with the spherical and hyperbolic cases.

``` r

distances <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5)
areas <- data.frame(distance = distances,
  Euclidean = geodesic_3d("e3", distance = distances)$area,
  Spherical = geodesic_3d("s3", distance = distances)$area,
  Hyperbolic = geodesic_3d("h3", distance = distances)$area)
knitr::kable(areas, digits = 3)
```

| distance | Euclidean | Spherical | Hyperbolic |
|---------:|----------:|----------:|-----------:|
|      0.5 |      0.25 |     0.230 |      0.272 |
|      1.0 |      1.00 |     0.708 |      1.381 |
|      1.5 |      2.25 |     0.995 |      4.534 |

## Identifying domain faces

A quotient identifies boundary faces of a fundamental domain, the region
used to represent the space. A ray crossing one face continues through
its paired face with its tangent transported by the pairing isometry.
This Euclidean example identifies the two x faces by translations of two
units.

``` r

to_left <- to_right <- diag(4)
to_left[1, 4] <- -2
to_right[1, 4] <- 2
faces <- list(
  thurston_portal_3d(c(1, 0, 0, 0), 1, to_left),
  thurston_portal_3d(c(-1, 0, 0, 0), 1, to_right))
```

Place a ball beyond the right-facing boundary in the identified space.
Repeated copies become visible along rays that cross the domain faces.
For other geometries, supply isometries in the embeddings documented by
[`thurston_portal_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/thurston_portal_3d.md)
and every paired face of the intended domain.

``` r

ggplot() + annotation_thurston_3d(centre = c(-0.5, 0, 1.5), radius = 0.3,
  fill = "#9E5E0F") + theme_void() +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raymarch", quotient = faces,
    fov = 110, max_distance = 5, dpi = 52, antialias = 1))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
